claims.text: Introducing controlled, uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates into a disordered magnetic high-entropy alloy increases its coercive field.
The initial material is a polycrystalline, disordered high-entropy alloy, such as an AlCoFeNi-based alloy.
A tailored thermal treatment can induce uniformly distributed nanoscale secondary-phase precipitates in the alloy.
The coercivity effect is expected to occur in room-temperature magnetic measurements.
The treated and baseline samples should have identical compositions and otherwise matched processing histories.
The structural mediator is a uniform distribution of nanoscale precipitates embedded in the alloy microstructure.
The precipitates act as effective domain-wall pinning centers.
Impeded domain-wall motion during magnetization reversal produces an increased coercive field.
The precipitate-forming treatment will yield a higher coercive field than an untreated matched baseline.
The baseline is the as-synthesized alloy without an additional precipitate-inducing thermal treatment.
The beneficial effect requires precipitates of an appropriate nanoscale size and a uniform distribution.
Precipitates that become too large, sparse, or inhomogeneous have diminished domain-wall-pinning efficiency.
The magnitude of the coercivity increase depends on precipitate size, distribution, and stability.
TEM or SEM can be used to assess precipitate formation, size, and uniformity.
Room-temperature hysteresis loops can be used to determine the coercive fields of the treated and baseline samples.
Failure of precipitate-bearing treated samples to show a statistically significant coercivity increase over the baseline would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The conditions require identical processing routes, while the intervention and experiment require one set to receive an additional thermal treatment and the baseline to remain untreated. This is only consistent if 'identical processing routes' means identical processing before the experimental heat-treatment intervention.
